subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 61-year-old man with chronic hypertension has had three attacks over the past year of sudden severe pain, redness, and swelling at the base of his right first metatarsophalangeal joint. He takes allopurinol for chronic gout. His blood pressure today is 152/94 mm Hg despite lifestyle modification.
question: Which of the following antihypertensive agents is contraindicated in this patient?
explanation_correct: Thiazide and loop diuretics can precipitate gout flares because they increase serum uric acid, so they are avoided in hypertensive patients with gout. For hypertension with gout, preferred agents are ACE inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, and ARBs (especially losartan). This patient's recurrent attacks at the first metatarsophalangeal joint are classic podagra.

explanation_incorrect.A: Losartan is one of the preferred agents in patients with hypertension and gout; ARBs, especially losartan, are explicitly recommended.
explanation_incorrect.B: Amlodipine, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, is an acceptable antihypertensive choice in patients with gout.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor, is listed among the preferred antihypertensive agents for patients with gout.
explanation_incorrect.D: Metoprolol is not identified as a cause of gout flares; the agents to avoid in gout are loop and thiazide diuretics.

educationalObjective: In hypertension with gout, avoid loop and thiazide diuretics because they cause gout flares; prefer ACE inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, or ARBs (especially losartan).

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 38-year-old woman with episodic headaches, palpitations, and drenching sweats is found to have a blood pressure of 214/126 mm Hg. Plasma free metanephrines are markedly elevated, and CT shows a 4-cm left adrenal mass. She is scheduled for adrenalectomy. Preoperatively, a β-blocker is prescribed for blood pressure control; 24 hours later her blood pressure rises to 240/140 mm Hg with severe headache.
question: Which of the following best explains the rise in blood pressure after β-blockade?

options.text: Beta2-receptor blockade causing bronchoconstriction and hypoxemia
Direct stimulation of catecholamine release by the beta-blocker
Alpha1-receptor upregulation unrelated to the beta-blocker
Rapid tolerance developing to the antihypertensive effect of the beta-blocker

explanation_correct: In pheochromocytoma, alpha-blockade must precede beta-blockade. When a beta-blocker is given first, the beta-mediated vasodilatory effects are blocked while the massive alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction driven by circulating catecholamines remains unopposed, causing a hypertensive crisis. Correct preparation uses phentolamine or phenoxybenzamine (alpha-blockade first) prior to resection and beta-blockade.

explanation_incorrect.B: Beta2 blockade causes bronchoconstriction in asthmatic patients; this patient has no lung disease and hypoxemia does not explain a blood pressure of 240/140 mm Hg.
explanation_incorrect.C: Beta-blockers do not stimulate catecholamine release by the tumor; the problem is loss of the beta-mediated vasodilatory counterbalance to alpha vasoconstriction.
explanation_incorrect.D: Alpha-receptor upregulation is not the mechanism; receptor number does not change within 24 hours of starting a beta-blocker.
explanation_incorrect.E: Tolerance to beta-blockers does not develop within a day; the acute worsening is a pharmacodynamic consequence of blocking beta receptors before alpha receptors.

educationalObjective: In pheochromocytoma, give alpha-blockade (phentolamine, phenoxybenzamine) before beta-blockade and resection; beta-blockade first causes unopposed alpha-mediated hypertensive crisis.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 28-year-old woman at 26 weeks' gestation has persistent blood pressures of 154 to 160/96 to 100 mm Hg on repeated measurements. She has no proteinuria and no symptoms of preeclampsia. The decision is made to begin antihypertensive therapy.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate antihypertensive medication?
explanation_correct: Antihypertensives appropriate in pregnancy include hydralazine, methyldopa, labetalol, and nifedipine. Labetalol is a safe, commonly used agent for chronic hypertension in pregnancy. ACE inhibitors and ARBs such as enalapril and valsartan are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal renal damage.

explanation_incorrect.A: Enalapril, an ACE inhibitor, is contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal toxicity, including renal failure and other fetal malformations.
explanation_incorrect.C: Thiazide diuretics are not among the agents recommended for hypertension in pregnancy, which are hydralazine, methyldopa, labetalol, and nifedipine.
explanation_incorrect.D: Valsartan, an ARB, is contraindicated in pregnancy for the same fetal renal reasons as ACE inhibitors.
explanation_incorrect.E: Spironolactone, an aldosterone antagonist, is not a recommended antihypertensive in pregnancy and can cause fetal feminization through antiandrogenic effects.

educationalObjective: Antihypertensives safe in pregnancy are hydralazine, methyldopa, labetalol, and nifedipine; ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus has a blood pressure of 152/96 mm Hg on two visits despite lifestyle modification. Urinalysis shows moderately increased albuminuria. He has no edema, orthopnea, or rales. The team chooses an antihypertensive that also provides kidney protection.
question: Which of the following medications is most appropriate because it is protective against diabetic nephropathy?
explanation_correct: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are protective against diabetic nephropathy and are first-line in diabetic patients with hypertension, particularly when albuminuria is present. lisinopril lowers glomerular pressure and reduces albuminuria, slowing progression of diabetic kidney disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Amlodipine is an acceptable antihypertensive in diabetes, but calcium channel blockers do not provide the specific protection against diabetic nephropathy that ACE inhibitors and ARBs do.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hydrochlorothiazide is an acceptable agent for hypertension with diabetes, but it is not the nephroprotective first-line choice when albuminuria is present.
explanation_incorrect.D: Metoprolol is an acceptable antihypertensive in diabetes but can mask hypoglycemia symptoms, and it does not protect against diabetic nephropathy.
explanation_incorrect.E: Clonidine is not listed among preferred agents for hypertension with diabetes and does not confer nephroprotection.

educationalObjective: In hypertension with diabetes, ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred because they are protective against diabetic nephropathy; beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemia symptoms.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 31-year-old woman with moderate persistent asthma is found to have a blood pressure of 150/96 mm Hg on two separate visits. She uses an inhaled corticosteroid and a short-acting beta2-agonist inhaler as needed. The decision is made to start antihypertensive therapy.
question: Which of the following antihypertensive agents should be avoided in this patient?
explanation_correct: Nonselective beta-blockers such as propranolol block beta2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle and can precipitate bronchoconstriction in patients with asthma, so they are avoided. Acceptable choices in hypertension with asthma are ARBs, calcium channel blockers, thiazide diuretics, and cardioselective beta-blockers. ACE inhibitors are also best avoided to prevent confusion between drug-induced cough and asthma-related cough.

explanation_incorrect.A: Losartan, an ARB, is listed among the preferred antihypertensive agents for patients with asthma.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hydrochlorothiazide, a thiazide diuretic, is an acceptable antihypertensive choice in patients with asthma.
explanation_incorrect.C: Amlodipine, a calcium channel blocker, is an acceptable and preferred antihypertensive agent in patients with asthma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Metoprolol is a cardioselective beta-blocker, which is acceptable in asthma, unlike nonselective agents.

educationalObjective: In hypertension with asthma, avoid nonselective beta-blockers (beta2-mediated bronchoconstriction) and ACE inhibitors; ARBs, CCBs, thiazides, and cardioselective beta-blockers are acceptable.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 52-year-old woman with hypertension is evaluated for back pain. Bone densitometry shows a T-score of -2.8 at the lumbar spine, consistent with osteoporosis. She has no diabetes, gout, or renal disease, and her blood pressure today is 156/96 mm Hg on no antihypertensive medications.
question: Which of the following is the preferred antihypertensive monotherapy in this patient?
explanation_correct: In hypertension with osteoporosis, thiazide diuretics are the preferred monotherapy because they increase calcium reabsorption, helping to preserve bone mineral density; an ACE inhibitor or ARB can be added if needed. This patient's osteoporosis makes a thiazide the ideal first agent.

explanation_incorrect.B: Furosemide, a loop diuretic, increases calcium excretion and would be counterproductive in a patient with osteoporosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Losartan is an acceptable antihypertensive but is not the preferred monotherapy in osteoporosis; it can be added to a thiazide if needed.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amlodipine is an acceptable antihypertensive but does not provide the bone-preserving benefit of increased calcium reabsorption that thiazides offer.
explanation_incorrect.E: Spironolactone is not identified as the preferred agent for hypertension with osteoporosis.

educationalObjective: In hypertension with osteoporosis, thiazides are the preferred monotherapy because they increase calcium reabsorption; combine with an ACE inhibitor or ARB if needed.
